title: IRIS: Integrated Reliability Imaging System
oneLiner: A five-camera inspection station designed to photograph every returned fuel cell column before teardown destroys the evidence of its field condition. I designed and built it, then handed it off to operations; the resolution, framing and coverage numbers here are the design targets it was built to hit.
cardSummary: Five-camera station designed to photograph returned fuel cell columns before teardown
metaDescription: I designed and built IRIS at Bloom Energy: a five-camera inspection station for returned fuel cell columns, concept to handoff, solo, in 8 weeks.
whatIOwnedSummary: I owned all of it. I set the optical specification and coverage geometry, designed the mechanics and registration scheme, built the capture software and operator console, ran procurement and vendor selection (407 components from seven suppliers), traced the camera-discovery failure, and wrote the handoff documentation set.

path.decision: Took sample photos of returned columns, which Reliability confirmed showed what they needed, then measured the plate thickness in pixels on those samples to work out the resolution the station required.
Imaged the outward face of all eight stacks on each column, one pedal press per face as the column is turned, and left the back faces for a later phase.
path.why: Reliability wanted complete evidence, back faces included, and Operations wanted as little delay as possible. One fixed tower can image the outward faces as the column turns; the back faces need a second, mirrored tower, which I left in the handoff as an open decision.

path.decision: Translated the 0.1 mm requirement into a 53 µm/px design target, using a 5 MP sensor, 35 mm lens, and a ±13 mm depth-of-field standoff window.
Chose five fixed cameras over one motorized camera.
path.why: Each face is captured in one pedal press with no moving parts in the image chain: no added time per unit, no drift, and no single point of failure.

path.decision: Handled dust and tint with controlled lighting and a color card in frame; designed the registration to hold framing within ±2.9 mm without touching production tooling.
Built the capture app with automated focus and exposure checks and per-unit override logs; verified gap-free five-camera coverage by script and tracked open items in the verification record.
Traced the camera-discovery failure to Windows Firewall on the managed laptops and delivered an exception package for IT and a commissioning runbook.
path.why: The fix needed a centrally applied exception under IT security review, and someone else would commission the station after my internship.

topMetrics.label: Handoff documents, including a verification record and a 19-decision design log

claims.title: Derived the optical spec at 53 µm/px from a 0.1 mm feature-resolution requirement
claims.requirementOrConstraint: Resolve roughly 0.1 mm of surface change across the full column face. Reliable detection needs about two pixels across the smallest feature, so one pixel cannot straddle an edge and average it away.
claims.method: Worked backwards from the requirement rather than from available hardware. The sampling rule set the required scale; frame width is fixed by the part, so dividing it across the sensor's pixel count gave the achievable scale. Aperture was then chosen for depth of field rather than brightness.
claims.resultMetric: The chain fixed sensor, lens, and working distance, and produced a ±13 mm standoff window that became the tolerance the mechanical design had to fit inside. Every later optical decision traces back to two inputs: the feature size and the frame width.
claims.limitations:
A design value computed from component specifications and frame geometry, never confirmed against a captured image.
Image a calibration target at the working distance and measure the actual field of view to confirm the achieved scale.

claims.title: Chose five fixed cameras by scripted layout comparison and verified gap-free coverage
claims.requirementOrConstraint: Every region of the outward face imaged head-on with no gaps, despite protruding features that shadow the regions Reliability cares about most. Had to fit within teardown takt time.
claims.method: Generated candidate layouts by script rather than laying them out by hand, and compared coverage for a single camera, for cameras centered on the protrusions, and for cameras with the protrusions at frame boundaries. Also evaluated a single camera on a motorized vertical stage.
claims.resultMetric: In the coverage script, putting the protrusions at frame boundaries instead of frame centers took coverage from about 90% to 100%. Boundary placement moves the hardest regions to mid-frame, where lighting and resolution are best, with overlap at every seam. Centering on the protrusions is the intuitive approach and leaves those regions shadowed. The motorized single-camera option was rejected on cycle time and on drift, since a moving stage on a dusty floor is both a repeatability risk and a single point of failure.
claims.limitations:
Coverage confirmed in geometry only, never checked against a physical column with cameras mounted.
Confirm the layout holds across column variants with differing module counts.

claims.title: Designed the registration to hold framing within ±2.9 mm with no contact to production tooling
claims.requirementOrConstraint: Framing had to stay inside the ±13 mm standoff window set by the optics, across carts that vary unit to unit, without adding fixturing or slowing teardown.
claims.method: Since a station that touches production tooling risks being shifted or damaged in daily use, I designed the registration to be entirely workpiece-referenced. Vertical position comes from a live-view band on a self-locking crank, depth from a projected laser gap cue, and rotation is set by eye to a band. I measured production carts (length, width, height, and how far each one sinks under a loaded unit, since the units are very heavy) so the crank and live-view band could absorb that variation. The coverage geometry sets the framing budget: ±2.9 mm before the overlap between neighboring camera views runs out.
claims.resultMetric: Roughly four times margin inside the optical standoff window. The cart is never clamped, docked, or modified, so teardown flow is unchanged and the station can be relocated without recalibration.
claims.limitations:
A budget from the coverage geometry, with the registration designed around my cart measurements. Nobody had positioned a loaded cart at the station before handoff, so it is not a spread measured on the line. By-eye rotation was not characterized across multiple operators before handoff.
Have several operators each position the same unit and measure the spread, to confirm the by-eye references hold across people rather than one person.

claims.title: Built the capture software end to end, gating every image on focus and exposure
claims.requirementOrConstraint: Cannot slow teardown, roughly one minute per unit. Has to work on an operator's first shift given high technician turnover, so the system must catch bad images rather than depend on anyone noticing them. Any override has to remain traceable.
claims.method: One pedal press fires all cameras simultaneously. Each image is scored for sharpness and exposure before acceptance; a failure flags that specific camera for individual re-fire rather than costing the whole capture. Overrides are written into the unit record alongside the image.
claims.resultMetric: A full unit runs from serial entry to completion in a browser, with per-camera retake. Every stored image carries its focus and exposure verdicts and any override flag, so the archive stays honest about which frames a human waved through.
claims.limitations:
Gate thresholds shipped as placeholders; the calibration tool exists, but calibration against real captures had not been done at handoff. Verified on simulated cameras only; no real camera, production or USB, had taken an image through it.
Time a full unit against takt with a real operator, which is the constraint the design was built around and the most important thing never measured.

claims.title: Made camera count configuration-driven and handed off a full commissioning package
claims.requirementOrConstraint: Someone else would commission and own the station after my internship. A two-column expansion, imaging two columns at once to double throughput, was under consideration. Vendor software versions change, so anything version-specific would go stale.
claims.method: Moved camera count, backend selection, and network tuning into a configuration file, and built three interchangeable camera backends covering production hardware, any USB camera, and a hardware-free simulator. Wrote a readiness script that tests the actual constraint rather than assuming a software version.
claims.resultMetric: End-to-end runs on simulated cameras verified at one, two, and five cameras, so the two-column expansion to ten cameras should need no software changes. Testing stopped at five cameras. I also wrote the six-point pass/fail test that closes commissioning, including ten five-camera bursts in a row with no incomplete images, every image at full sensor resolution, a deliberately defocused lens caught by the focus gate and fixed with a single-camera retake, and a full unit run through the console by foot pedal. The handoff was seven documents: a handoff memo with status and ownership, a commissioning runbook, the firewall exception package for IT, a decision log of 19 locked design choices, a verification record with 13 open items (each naming the event that closes it), a code guide written for a non-programmer working with an AI assistant, and an asset inventory.
claims.limitations:
The handoff had not been exercised when I left. Nobody had brought the station up using only the documentation, so gaps in it are unknown.
Have the new owner do a dry run from the runbook alone and record every point where they get stuck.

outcome: Built and handed off to operations eight weeks after the project started. At handoff the tower was built, all 407 components had arrived, and the five cameras were powered and linked to the network, but no image had been taken. The capture software runs end to end on simulated cameras: a full unit goes from serial entry through focus- and exposure-gated capture in a browser, at one, two and five cameras. Commissioning on the line was blocked because Bloom's managed Windows laptops dropped the cameras' discovery replies. I traced it to the packet level, found that the exception had to be applied centrally by IT, and reproduced it on a second, freshly imaged laptop with IT watching. That shows the firewall alone is enough to stop discovery, not that it is the only fault. I delivered the exception package and runbook before handoff, so the resolution, framing and coverage figures above remain design targets rather than measurements from the line.

interfaces.notes: One cable per camera carries both power and data. Expansion to ten cameras is additional ports rather than a topology change.

GigE Vision on an isolated subnet with no gateway and no route to the corporate network. Corporate connectivity uses a separate adapter on the same machine. Discovery replies crossed this link and were dropped by the PC's own firewall after they arrived.
Single keystroke triggers a capture, so the operator's hands stay on the cart. Deliberately the only physical input in the workflow.
Images written under the unit serial, each carrying its focus and exposure verdicts and any operator override. This is the record of what happened, not just the pictures.
Serial-to-image linkage defined as the next integration step. Images are serial-tagged on the station in the interim, so nothing is lost if the integration lands later.
No physical contact, by design. A station that touches production tooling risks being shifted or damaged in daily use, so all registration is workpiece-referenced.

evidence.label: Showcase poster
evidence.note: Intern showcase poster, August 2026, made before commissioning: requirements, optical derivation chain, five-camera coverage comparison, station CAD render, and the operator console. Three lines on it describe the plan rather than results: no unit had been imaged yet, so the 'complete evidence stream' is the intent; registration had not been checked with a loaded cart; and filing images to the MES was the next integration step.

evidence.label: Commissioning package
evidence.note: Seven documents: handoff memo, commissioning runbook, firewall exception package, decision log, verification record with open items, code guide, and asset inventory. Internal; not publicly released.

projectRisks: Commissioning was not completed before handoff. Camera discovery was blocked at handoff by the host firewall on the corporate-managed laptops, and the fix needed a centrally applied exception under IT security review. I traced it to the specific rule and blocked process and delivered the exception package and runbook. I showed the block is enough on its own to stop discovery; whether anything else is wrong won't be known until the exception is applied. Ticket ownership transferred to my manager before I left.

The production camera driver was never exercised against real hardware. I built a simulator backend to verify the full pipeline end to end, a USB-webcam backend for demos and operator training, and a readiness script that isolates which layer is failing at bring-up.

Focus and exposure thresholds shipped as placeholders, since real values depend on real optics and lighting. The calibration tool and procedure are built and documented in the runbook; running it on real captures was left for commissioning.

Optical resolution and framing budget are design values, not measurements taken with the system running on the line. The framing budget comes from the coverage geometry, and the registration was designed around measured cart dimensions and how far carts sink under a loaded unit.

Phase 1 images the outward face only, a scope decision to hit the timeline. The software should support the extension unmodified (tested to five cameras), so adding it is a fixturing problem rather than a redesign.

lessons.text: I was project owner, mechanical designer, software engineer, and network debugger at once, so every trade-off went through me. Choosing an aperture for depth of field was also choosing how precisely an operator would have to position a cart. Owning both ends made those couplings visible in a way a specialist role would not have.

Reliability and Operations each set constraints that shaped the design fundamentally. Reliability needing every region imaged is what drove the five-camera layout. I learned to find the binding constraint from each group early rather than designing and then seeking approval.

Procurement shaped the build as much as the analysis did. The requirement picked the camera and lens, but supplier onboarding decided where the lens came from, and the station PC's lead time forced the software to run on any host. Treating procurement as an engineering input rather than an administrative step would have changed my sequencing from the start.

Designing the handoff early changed what I built. Knowing I would not be the one commissioning the station is why camera count is set in a configuration file (as opposed to being hard-coded), and why the readiness check prints fixes rather than error codes.

IT was the stakeholder I did not think to consult. Reliability and Operations were obvious sources of requirements; the corporate network was infrastructure I assumed would just work. It became the binding constraint. On any project touching managed IT systems, I would have a meeting with them outlining the requirements of the project in week one.
